note: Shibuya's daily life (issue #357): the people to know, their hours, the jobs, the counters and the calendar. Built into web/data/shibuya/life.json by pipeline/life.py, which resolves every place. Facts in 'fact' are checked against the sources in docs/cities/shibuya.md.

bonds.title: The guide
bonds.busy: I've a group in ten minutes. Catch me in the daytime or early evening, when the light's on the crossing.

ranks.title: The valley
ranks.invite: You crossed like someone who's done it before. Have you a little of the {slot} to spare? I'll show you why this place is where it is.
talk: Stand still a second and feel the ground. Every road here runs downhill to this spot. Shibuya is the bottom of a valley: the name says so, 谷, valley.
That's why the Ginza Line, a subway, pulls in on the third floor. The train stays level; the ground drops away under it.
ranks.fact: Shibuya Station sits at the bottom of a valley, so the Ginza Line subway arrives above the street, on the third floor.

ask.q: So where do you think the river went?

options.reply: Right. The Shibuya River runs in a culvert under the station and comes back into daylight by Shibuya Stream, to the south. Go and look some time.
It's still there, in a culvert under the station. It comes up again by Shibuya Stream, to the south.

request.text: See where the river comes back up, by Shibuya Stream
request.ask: Been down to Shibuya Stream yet? The river comes out from under the station there.

ranks.title: A word with the cabbies
talk: You found the river. Most people who live here never have.
I started as a bus guide: flag, whistle, forty people from Sendai. The drivers on the rank by Hachiko still know me. I've told them you're with me.
ranks.fact: The Shibuya River reappears from its culvert at Shibuya Stream, south of the station, where its banks were rebuilt as a walk in 2018.

gives.name: A word with the cabbies
gives.text: 30% off every taxi and ride in Shibuya

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Try your eye on a tower first: pick one, press G, and tell me how close you got.

ranks.title: Three thousand a green
talk: Count the people on the next green. At the busiest change it's up to three thousand, from five directions, and nobody collides.
It became a scramble in 1973. Before that, people here waited twice to get across to the far corner.
ranks.fact: Shibuya's crossing has been a scramble, with every arm red at once for traffic, since 1973.

ask.q: Why does nobody collide, do you think?

options.reply: That's it exactly. Nobody looks at feet; they look at the gap two people ahead and lean into it. You already walk like that.
Only at New Year and Halloween. The rest of the year it's just people looking two steps ahead.

request.text: Stand with Hachiko at night, when the square empties
request.ask: Go and stand with Hachiko after dark, when the square thins out. He's a different dog then.

ranks.title: The second Hachiko
talk: You went at night. Good. Then you'll have noticed how small he is.
That statue is the second one. The first, from 1934, was melted down in the war for its metal. This one is from 1948, made by the first sculptor's son.
Hachiko himself was there in 1934, at the unveiling of his own statue. He died the next March.
ranks.fact: The Hachiko statue is the second: the 1934 original was melted down in wartime, and Ando Takeshi, the first sculptor's son, made this one in 1948.

gives.name: Aoi's introduction
gives.text: 20% more for every job in Shibuya

request.ask: Keep walking. When you can point to Yoyogi from here without looking, come back.

ranks.title: Your own tour
talk: I've been listening to you. You say what a place is, then what it was, then where to stand. That's the whole job.
Next month I'm short a guide on Saturdays. I'm not offering. I'm saying you could.
Whatever you do next: when someone asks you the way, don't point. Walk the first ten steps with them.
ranks.fact: A scramble crossing stops every car at once and lets people cross in all directions, the diagonal included; Japan's first were laid out in the late 1960s.

bonds.title: The shop on Center Gai
bonds.busy: Shop's open, hands are full. Come by in the evening, or late: this street doesn't close.

ranks.title: Basketball Street
ranks.invite: You keep looking up at the arch. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll tell you what it used to say.
talk: In 2011 the shopkeepers renamed this Basketball Street. New arch, new signs. They wanted a cleaner name for it.
Nobody ever called it that. Not once. The arch says Center Gai again because the street won.
ranks.fact: Center Gai was officially renamed Basketball Street in 2011; everyone went on calling it Center Gai.

ask.q: What would you have called it?

options.reply: Ha. You'd have saved them the cost of an arch.
That's what they thought. The street disagreed.

ranks.title: A run for the shop
talk: Half my stock is American, 1970s, bought by the bale. The other half comes from grandmothers' wardrobes in Setagaya.
I need a pair of legs. A jacket promised to the desk at SKY GATE before the lifts get busy. It pays, and you'd see how fast you really are.
ranks.fact: Shibuya's vintage clothes shops grew up in the 1990s in the backstreets between Center Gai, Harajuku and Shimokitazawa.

gives.name: Shun's runner
gives.text: A paid delivery from the shop, in your diary under Work

request.text: Run the jacket to SKY GATE for Shun
request.ask: The jacket's bagged and waiting. It's in your diary, under Work.

talk: On time. I knew it.
See the silver cylinder up the hill? 109. Opened in 1979, and the name is a pun: ten is 'to', nine is 'kyu'. Tokyu, the railway that built it.
In the nineties the girls who shopped there set what all of Japan wore. I was nine and thought they were the coolest people alive.
ranks.fact: SHIBUYA109 opened in 1979; its name reads to-kyu, ten-nine, after Tokyu, the railway company that built it.

request.text: Photograph 109 from the street (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Take me a picture of 109 from the foot of the hill. Photo mode, then come back.

ranks.title: The screens
talk: Good shot. You stood where the two roads split: everyone does, without knowing why.
QFRONT, over there with the big screen, opened in December 1999. Before it, the crossing was just a crossing. The screens made it a place people film.
ranks.fact: QFRONT, the glass building with the great screen over the scramble, opened in December 1999.

gives.name: A shopkeeper's eye
gives.text: Eye: you size things up faster

request.text: Eat something standing up, like everyone here does
request.ask: Have you eaten? There's standing soba by the station. Go on, then tell me I'm wrong.

ranks.title: Five in the morning
talk: Soba. Good. Now you're from here.
I said this street never sleeps. It does, for about an hour, around five. The last trains have gone, the first haven't come, and the crows have the whole place.
Stay up for it once. It's the only time you can hear the crossing's signals from here.
ranks.fact: The last trains leave Shibuya a little after half past midnight and the first run from about half past four.

gives.name: Regular's rate
gives.text: 15% more for every job in Shibuya

bonds.title: The photographer on the roof
bonds.busy: Not now: the light's wrong. I'm up here at golden hour, when it's dry. The roof shuts in the rain.

ranks.title: 229 metres
ranks.invite: You came up for the light, not the selfie. Have you some of the {slot}? Stand here.
talk: 229 metres over the street. On a clear winter evening Fuji stands there, in the west, a hundred kilometres off, and the sun goes down beside it.
Everyone shoots the crossing straight down. Turn round. The picture is the light on Shinjuku's towers, behind you.
ranks.fact: SHIBUYA SKY, the roof of Shibuya Scramble Square, is about 229 m above the street and opened on 1 November 2019.

ask.q: When would you shoot from here?

options.reply: Blue hour. The sky and the windows are the same brightness for ten minutes, and that's the whole secret.
At noon it's a map. Come twenty minutes after sunset: the sky and the windows match, for ten minutes.

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Show me one frame taken in the good light: golden hour, or just after sunset.

ranks.title: Night film
talk: That's it. You waited for it.
I learned on film that was balanced for tungsten light. It turns street lamps white and the sky deep blue. Here: I've set your camera up the same way for after dark.
ranks.fact: Blue hour, when the sky's brightness matches lit windows, lasts only some ten to twenty minutes after sunset at Tokyo's latitude.

gives.name: Night film
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out on Taro's tungsten film

ranks.title: The gymnasium
talk: Look north-west. The roof like two commas: Yoyogi National Gymnasium, Tange Kenzo, for the 1964 Olympics.
The roof hangs from cables, like a suspension bridge. No columns inside. He drew it and then they had to work out whether it would stand.
ranks.fact: Yoyogi National Gymnasium, by Tange Kenzo for the 1964 Olympics, hangs its roof from steel cables like a suspension bridge.

needs.text: Shoot more first. Come back when you can tell me where the shadow of this building falls at four.

request.text: Photograph the four faces of the crossing
request.ask: There's a little commission in your diary: four subjects round the crossing. Do it properly.

ranks.title: The mural
talk: You've an eye. So: the best picture in Shibuya isn't a view at all.
In the passage to the Inokashira Line hangs Okamoto Taro's Myth of Tomorrow. Thirty metres long. Painted in Mexico in 1968, lost for thirty years, found in a yard outside Mexico City in 2003.
It's been here since 2008, and three hundred thousand people a day walk past it looking at their phones.
ranks.fact: Okamoto Taro's 30 m mural Myth of Tomorrow, painted in Mexico in 1968-69 and lost until 2003, has hung in Shibuya Station's Mark City passage since 2008.

gives.name: Taro's eye
gives.text: Light, from someone who waits for it

ranks.title: The last frame
talk: I've shot this roof four hundred evenings. I keep one frame a year.
This year's is of you, at the edge, looking the wrong way: at Shinjuku. I'll print it.
Keep one a year. Throw the rest away. That's all I know.
ranks.fact: From SHIBUYA SKY, Mount Fuji stands about 100 km to the west-south-west and shows best on clear winter mornings and evenings.

bonds.title: The Sangenjaya local
bonds.busy: I'm at work till the evening. Find me here after, any night.

ranks.title: Three teahouses
ranks.invite: You've walked all the way out here? Then you've earned it. Got a little of the {slot}?
talk: Sangenjaya: three teahouses. In the Edo days the road to Mount Oyama forked here, and three teahouses stood at the fork for the pilgrims: Shigaraki, Kadoya and Tanakaya.
The fork is still there. It's the junction under the expressway, where Route 246 and Setagaya-dori split.
ranks.fact: Sangenjaya means three teahouses: Shigaraki, Kadoya and Tanakaya, which stood where the Oyama pilgrims' road forked, now the junction of Route 246 and Setagaya-dori.

ask.q: Which do you think lasted longest?

options.text: The one with the family name
options.reply: Tanakaya. It became a ceramics shop and was still trading by the junction into this century. Good guess.
Tanakaya did: it became a ceramics shop and traded on by the junction into this century.

ranks.title: The carrot
talk: That orange tower is Carrot Tower. 1996, 124 metres, and the name was chosen from children's entries.
The top floor is free. Nobody tells the tourists. You can see Fuji from the lobby, with a coffee, for nothing.
ranks.fact: Carrot Tower in Sangenjaya, finished in 1996 and about 124 m tall, has a free observation lobby on its 26th floor; its name came from a public competition.

request.text: Walk to the foot of Carrot Tower
request.ask: Have you been over to the Carrot yet? Five minutes, past the tram stop.

ranks.title: The tram
talk: You'll have seen the little tram under the tower. The Setagaya Line: ten stops, five kilometres, two cars. It's one of only two tram lines left in Tokyo.
I've an errand that needs doing most evenings: clean towels from the shop to the bathhouse. It's yours if you want it.
ranks.fact: The Tokyu Setagaya Line runs 5 km and ten stops from Sangenjaya to Shimo-Takaido, one of Tokyo's two surviving tram lines.

gives.name: The towel run
gives.text: A paid errand in Sangenjaya, in your diary under Work

request.ask: The towels are bundled by Hanamasa. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The bath
talk: Mr Tanaka says you were quick. He doesn't say much, so that's a medal.
A public bath in Tokyo costs 550 yen, the same at every one: the price is set for the whole city. There were over two thousand six hundred of them in 1968. Under five hundred now.
ranks.fact: A sento in Tokyo charges a fixed 550 yen; the city had about 2,700 in 1968 and has fewer than 500 today.

gives.name: A local's table
gives.text: Taste: you know where people here really go

ranks.title: The triangle
talk: Come out to the triangle with me: the block of alleys between the two big roads. Sixty-odd bars in a wedge you can walk round in four minutes.
It grew out of the black market after the war, and they keep saying it'll be redeveloped. Every year it's still here.
If it goes, I'll tell you first. Until then you've a seat.
ranks.fact: Sangenjaya's Sankaku Chitai, the triangle of alleys between Route 246 and Setagaya-dori, grew from a post-war black market and still holds dozens of tiny bars.

gives.name: A seat in the triangle
gives.text: 15% more for every job in Sangenjaya and Shibuya

jobs.title: Which way from Hachiko?
jobs.blurb: Visitors at the statue ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: A visitor with a paper map

jobs.title: Four faces of the crossing
jobs.blurb: A magazine wants QFRONT, 109, Hachiko and Scramble Square. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: The picture editor writes back: 'More like these.'

jobs.title: A jacket for SKY GATE
jobs.blurb: From Shun's shop on Center Gai to the desk at SKY GATE, across the scramble, before the evening lifts fill.
jobs.text: One 1974 flight jacket, bagged. Mind the scramble: wait for the green.

jobs.title: A fare to Harajuku
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up at the Hachiko kerb and take your passenger up Meiji-dori to Harajuku.
jobs.who: A stylist with three garment bags
jobs.text: "Harajuku, the Takeshita end. I'm late for a fitting."

jobs.title: Towels for Chiyo-no-yu
jobs.blurb: Clean towels from the shop by Hanamasa to the bathhouse, before the evening regulars arrive.
jobs.text: Forty towels, still warm from the dryer.
jobs.done: Mr Tanaka nods at the stack.

shops.name: Standing soba 立ち食いそば
shops.hello: Irasshai. Ticket machine's broken: tell me.

menu.name: Kake soba
menu.text: Buckwheat noodles in dark Kanto broth, eaten standing, in about four minutes. Tokyo's broth is soy and bonito, darker than Osaka's.

menu.name: Tempura soba
menu.text: A round kakiage fritter on top, going soft in the broth on purpose. Standing soba began on railway platforms in the 1890s, for people with a train to catch.

shops.name: Vending machines 自販機
shops.hello: A row of lit buttons. Red labels are hot, blue are cold.

menu.name: Fruit milk
menu.text: The after-bath drink: cold fruit milk, one hand on your hip. Every bathhouse in Japan sells it.

menu.name: Hot corn soup
menu.text: A can of hot corn potage, sold from the red buttons from autumn to spring. Japan has about one vending machine for every thirty people.

menu.name: Strawberry and cream crêpe
menu.text: Rolled into a cone so you can walk with it. Harajuku's crêpe stands opened on Takeshita-dori in 1977 and never left.

menu.name: A Hachiko charm
menu.text: A small brass Akita on a red cord. For waiting well.

events.title: Hatsumode at Meiji Jingu
events.where: The south gate of Meiji Jingu, Harajuku
events.verb: Join the queue for the first visit of the year
events.text: The first shrine visit of the year. About three million people come here in the first three days, more than to any other shrine in Japan.
lines: The gravel path is full from edge to edge and moves at the pace of the slowest grandmother. Police with lit signs hold the crowd in blocks.
At the hall you throw a coin, bow twice, clap twice, bow once. About three million people do it here in the first three days of January.
On the way out, last year's charms go on the fire and this year's fortune costs a hundred yen.

events.title: Hanami in Yoyogi Park
events.text: Blue sheets under about six hundred cherry trees. Tokyo's Somei-Yoshino open in the last days of March in most years and are full about a week later.
lines: Blue tarpaulins, corner to corner. The youngest person from each office has been here since six this morning holding the spot.
Somei-Yoshino are all clones of one tree, which is why a whole park opens in the same week and drops in the same wind.

events.title: Omotesando illumination
events.native: 表参道イルミネーション
events.text: The zelkovas of Omotesando, the kilometre-long approach to Meiji Jingu, strung with warm lights from sunset.
lines: About a hundred and fifty zelkovas, lit from the trunks up, for a kilometre. The avenue was laid out in 1920 as the approach to Meiji Jingu.
The footbridges are closed to stop people standing on them for the photograph. Everyone takes it from the kerb instead.

events.title: Halloween: not at the crossing
events.text: The ward asks people not to come to Shibuya for Halloween. Drinking in the street round the station is banned from 18:00 to 05:00, all year.
lines: Banners on every rail: 'Shibuya is not a venue for Halloween events.' Hachiko is boxed in behind white hoardings for the night.
Since October 2024, drinking in the streets round the station is banned from six in the evening to five in the morning, every day of the year.

events.title: New Year's Eve: no countdown
events.verb: Wait for midnight at the kerb
events.text: The countdown at the crossing has been cancelled every year since 2020. At midnight the lights simply change.
lines: No stage, no countdown: it has been cancelled every year since 2020. The crossing's lights change at midnight as they do at any other minute.
The bells are elsewhere: a hundred and eight strokes at the temples, one for each worldly desire, the last one falling in the new year.
